prompt: Why is password reuse considered the single biggest real-world account-compromise risk?
choices: It makes passwords easier to guess through brute force
A breach at one low-value site hands attackers a credential pair they can replay against your email, bank, and other accounts via credential stuffing
It slows down your browser's autofill feature
Reused passwords are always shorter than unique ones

prompt: What is the main reason SMS-based 2FA is considered weaker than TOTP apps or hardware security keys?
choices: SMS messages are not encrypted during transmission
SMS codes are too short to be secure
A phone number can be hijacked via a SIM swap at the carrier, redirecting codes to the attacker without touching the victim's device
SMS codes never expire

prompt: In the example phishing email ('Your mailbox storage is full'), which detail is the most reliable red flag?
choices: The email uses the word 'Dear'
The sender's actual domain (e.g. company-mail-secure.net) does not match the real organization's domain, even though the display name says 'IT Support'
The email was sent on a weekday
The subject line contains the word 'Action'

prompt: What does the HTTPS padlock icon in a browser actually guarantee?
choices: The site is verified safe and free of malware
The business running the site has been identity-checked
The connection between your browser and the server is encrypted and matches the certificate's domain name — nothing about the site's trustworthiness
The site cannot be a phishing site

prompt: After checking your email on Have I Been Pwned and finding it listed in a breach, what is the correct next step?
choices: Delete your email account immediately
Ignore it since breach notification sites are rarely accurate
Change the password at the breached site and anywhere else you reused that same password, then enable 2FA if not already on
Change your email address to a new provider

prompt: Why does a 5-6 word random passphrase (like 'horse-battery-lantern-plum-gravel7') tend to be stronger than a short complex-looking password like 'P@ssw0rd!23'?
choices: Because it contains more special characters
Because its length and true randomness produce more entropy, making it far harder to crack despite looking simpler
Because passphrases are automatically hashed differently by servers
Because dictionary words can never appear in password-cracking wordlists

prompt: What makes a FIDO2 hardware key like a YubiKey more phishing-resistant than a TOTP app code?
choices: It generates longer numeric codes
It requires a fingerprint instead of a code
It cryptographically binds the login challenge to the real website's domain, so a lookalike phishing site cannot complete the authentication even if the user is fooled
It never needs to be plugged in or touched

prompt: Which of the following is an acceptable target for the hands-on exercises in this Tier 0 module?
choices: A coworker's social media account, with their verbal permission
Your own accounts, your own isolated lab environment, or a named legal practice platform you're authorized to use
A small business website you found that looks outdated
A public Wi-Fi network at a coffee shop, just to observe traffic
